## Proof that $\phi(n) = \Theta(n)$

### Upper Bound: $\phi(n) \leq 3n$

Consider the $n$ axis-parallel planes $\Pi_k = \{(k, y, z) : y, z \in [n]\}$ for $k = 1, \dots, n$. If any $\Pi_k$ contained 4 selected points, those 4 would be coplanar, violating the condition. So each $\Pi_k$ contains at most 3 selected points, giving:

$$\phi(n) \leq 3n.$$

### Lower Bound: $\phi(n) \geq n/2$

**Construction.** Let $p$ be a prime with $p \leq n$. By Bertrand's postulate, for $n \geq 2$ there exists a prime $p$ with $n/2 < p \leq n$. Define $p$ points in $\{0, 1, \dots, p-1\}^3 \subseteq \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}^3$:

$$P_t = \bigl(t,\; t^2 \bmod p,\; t^3 \bmod p\bigr), \quad t = 0, 1, \dots, p-1.$$

**Claim.** No four of these points are coplanar.

*Proof of claim.* Take four distinct points $P_{t_1}, P_{t_2}, P_{t_3}, P_{t_4}$ with $t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4 \in \{0, \dots, p-1\}$ all distinct. They are coplanar if and only if the determinant

$$D = \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & t_1 & (t_1^2 \bmod p) & (t_1^3 \bmod p) \\ 1 & t_2 & (t_2^2 \bmod p) & (t_2^3 \bmod p) \\ 1 & t_3 & (t_3^2 \bmod p) & (t_3^3 \bmod p) \\ 1 & t_4 & (t_4^2 \bmod p) & (t_4^3 \bmod p) \end{pmatrix}$$

equals zero. Since every entry is an integer, $D \in \mathbb{Z}$. Reducing the matrix entries modulo $p$:

$$D \equiv \det\begin{pmatrix} 1 & t_1 & t_1^2 & t_1^3 \\ 1 & t_2 & t_2^2 & t_2^3 \\ 1 & t_3 & t_3^2 & t_3^3 \\ 1 & t_4 & t_4^2 & t_4^3 \end{pmatrix} = \prod_{1 \le i < j \le 4}(t_j - t_i) \pmod{p}.$$

This is the Vandermonde determinant. Since $t_1, t_2, t_3, t_4$ are distinct elements of $\{0, \dots, p-1\}$, they are distinct modulo $p$, so each factor $(t_j - t_i) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$. Since $p$ is prime:

$$\prod_{i < j}(t_j - t_i) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}.$$

Therefore $D \not\equiv 0 \pmod{p}$, which forces $D \neq 0$ as an integer. Hence the four points are **not** coplanar. $\square$

This construction yields $p$ points with no four coplanar, so $\phi(n) \geq p > n/2$.

### Conclusion

Combining both bounds:

$$\frac{n}{2} < \phi(n) \leq 3n \quad \text{for all } n \geq 2,$$

which establishes

$$\phi(n) = \Theta(n).$$

The trivial upper bound of $3n$ **cannot** be improved to $o(n)$, since the modular construction proves $\phi(n) = \Omega(n)$. The key idea is that the Vandermonde determinant — which vanishes only when four parameters coincide — remains nonzero modulo a prime $p$, and since the determinant is an integer, nonvanishing mod $p$ implies nonvanishing over $\mathbb{R}$. This bridges the gap between coplanarity over $\mathbb{F}_p$ (which the modular construction controls) and coplanarity over $\mathbb{R}$ (which the problem requires).
